scenarios.title: Internal reconnaissance (host/port sweep, LDAP & share enumeration)
scenarios.expected_observation: One workstation sweeps the server subnet, scans ports, dumps the directory and enumerates shares: a sensor should flag internal scanning and bulk directory queries from a single host.
steps: The compromised workstation pings the server subnet to find live hosts.
It runs one fast SYN scan across common ports on the victim servers, most probes unanswered or reset.
It dumps users, computers, groups, SPNs and OUs from the domain controller over LDAP.
It lists shares on each server over SMB (srvsvc); only the traffic is visible, not the attacker's intent.

scenarios.title: Lateral movement (RDP, SMB admin-share PsExec, WMI)
scenarios.expected_observation: A workstation reaches servers with RDP, admin-share service execution and WMI: a sensor should flag workstation-to-server admin protocols that the baseline never carries.
steps: The foothold workstation opens RDP sessions to servers, which workstations do not normally do.
It writes a service binary to the ADMIN$ share and starts it through the service control manager (PsExec style).
It runs commands remotely through WMI over DCOM on port 135.
A second popped workstation repeats the same techniques; what ran on the target is not visible, only the admin traffic.

scenarios.title: Credential access (Kerberoasting, AS-REP roast, spray, DCSync)
scenarios.expected_observation: Kerberoasting, AS-REP roasting, a password spray and a DCSync from a non-domain-controller: a sensor should raise Kerberos and directory-replication detections against one workstation.
steps: A burst of service ticket requests asks for RC4 only (Kerberoasting).
AS-REQ without pre-authentication for several accounts (AS-REP roasting).
Many accounts fail pre-authentication with one password (spray).
A directory replication request (DsGetNCChanges) comes from a host that is not a domain controller (DCSync); cracked secrets are not visible.

scenarios.title: C2 beaconing (RMM cloud + low-and-slow HTTPS + ngrok tunnel)
scenarios.expected_observation: A workstation makes a first-time remote-access (RMM) connection, beacons on a jittered interval to a known C2 and holds a long tunnel: a sensor should flag the RMM, the periodic beacon and the persistent opaque tunnel.
steps: A first-time connection to a remote-management cloud service appears.
Small HTTPS check-ins to a C2 host repeat roughly every minute with jitter all window long.
A persistent TLS tunnel to a tunnelling service is opened and held for at least an hour.
Payloads are TLS-encrypted, so only cadence, destination and volume are observable.

scenarios.title: DNS tunneling (long encoded TXT queries via the resolver)
scenarios.expected_observation: Long encoded subdomain queries and TXT responses at high volume to one attacker name server: a sensor should flag DNS tunnelling by query length, entropy and volume.
steps: The workstation sends bursts of queries with long base32-looking labels under one parent domain.
Queries go through the internal resolver, which recurses toward an attacker-controlled name server.
Answers return as TXT records carrying payload.
Burst after burst with random gaps; the data inside the labels is encoded, so what was moved is not visible.
scenarios.notes: Category is a judgement: DNS tunnelling is also command and control in common taxonomies; placed under Exfiltration to balance the taxonomy. The code does not say which use the traffic models.

scenarios.title: Data staging & exfiltration (SMB staging then HTTPS upload)
scenarios.expected_observation: Bulk SMB reads from file and backup servers followed by a large asymmetric HTTPS upload to external object storage: a sensor should flag staging and an outbound transfer far above normal.
steps: The workstation pulls large volumes from a department share over SMB.
It reads a database or user share on the backup server in the same way.
After staging it resolves a cloud-storage name and opens a TLS session.
A long chunked upload of PUT requests runs with a ramp and one pause; the content is encrypted.

scenarios.title: Scattered Spider kill chain (recon->creds->lateral->C2->exfil)
scenarios.expected_observation: A full kill chain from one workstation (scan, credentials, lateral movement, C2, DNS tunnel, staging, upload): a sensor should show several correlated detections on the same host over about two hours.
steps: C2 beaconing starts first and runs for the whole window.
Recon, then credential attacks, then lateral movement run in consecutive phases.
DNS tunnelling overlaps the end of lateral movement.
The chain ends with SMB staging and a large HTTPS upload; there is no encryption or wiper stage.
scenarios.notes: Multi-tactic chain. Terminal stage is exfiltration, so it is filed there; also_categories lists the other tactics.

scenarios.title: Ransomware encryption write-storm (SMB in-place encrypt + .ext)
scenarios.expected_observation: A write-storm over SMB: files are read and rewritten in place, renamed with a .akira extension, and a ransom note is dropped on the shares: a sensor should flag mass modification and rename on file servers.
steps: The workstation opens a share and lists the directory.
Each file is opened with read, write and delete access and rewritten block by block.
Each file is renamed to carry the .akira extension in the same handle.
A ransom note lands in its own short SMB session per directory; the encryption itself is not observable, only its I/O.

scenarios.title: Cobalt Strike C2 (HTTP jittered beacon + SMB named-pipe P2P)
scenarios.expected_observation: A jittered HTTPS beacon to a Cobalt Strike team server plus SMB named-pipe peer beacons between internal servers: a sensor should flag the periodic beacon and internal named-pipe sessions.
steps: The workstation checks in over HTTPS to the team server on a jittered interval.
Beacon requests are small and use a pinned profile (one URI, one user agent).
Two or three servers each hold one long-lived SMB named-pipe session (msagent style) from the workstation.
Pipe sessions are polled with small framed reads and writes; commands and results are not readable.

scenarios.title: Akira ransomware kill chain (CISA AA24-109A)
scenarios.expected_observation: A ransomware kill chain from one workstation (C2, recon, credentials, lateral movement, exfiltration, then encryption with the .akira extension): a sensor should show correlated detections ending in a write-storm.
steps: C2 starts first: RMM cloud, a Cloudflare tunnel and an ngrok-style tunnel for C2; the exfil upload uses an rclone user agent.
Recon, credential access and lateral movement follow in order.
A large HTTPS upload to external storage follows the staging reads.
The chain ends with an SMB read/rewrite/rename storm (.akira) on the file and backup servers; the ransom note is written to the shares, but the cryptography is not visible.
scenarios.notes: Shares one chain builder with the other actor scenarios; they differ in C2 style, file extension and note text. Multi-tactic; filed under its end state.

scenarios.title: Medusa ransomware kill chain (CISA AA25-071A)
scenarios.expected_observation: A ransomware kill chain from one workstation (C2, recon, credentials, lateral movement, exfiltration, then encryption with the .medusa extension): a sensor should show correlated detections ending in a write-storm.
steps: C2 starts first: a Cloudflared tunnel, a persistent Ligolo-style TLS tunnel and jittered HTTPS check-ins for C2.
Recon, credential access and lateral movement follow in order.
A large HTTPS upload to external storage follows the staging reads.
The chain ends with an SMB read/rewrite/rename storm (.medusa) on the file and backup servers; the ransom note is written to the shares, but the cryptography is not visible.
scenarios.notes: Shares one chain builder with the other actor scenarios; they differ in C2 style, file extension and note text. Multi-tactic; filed under its end state.

scenarios.title: Black Basta ransomware kill chain (CISA AA24-131A)
scenarios.expected_observation: A ransomware kill chain from one workstation (C2, recon, credentials, lateral movement, exfiltration, then encryption with the .basta extension): a sensor should show correlated detections ending in a write-storm.
steps: C2 starts first: Cobalt Strike HTTP and SMB-pipe C2 to its own team server.
Recon, credential access and lateral movement follow in order.
A large HTTPS upload to external storage follows the staging reads.
The chain ends with an SMB read/rewrite/rename storm (.basta) on the file and backup servers; the ransom note is written to the shares, but the cryptography is not visible.
scenarios.notes: Shares one chain builder with the other actor scenarios; they differ in C2 style, file extension and note text. Multi-tactic; filed under its end state.

scenarios.title: Play ransomware kill chain (CISA AA23-352A)
scenarios.expected_observation: A ransomware kill chain from one workstation (C2, recon, credentials, lateral movement, exfiltration, then encryption with the .play extension): a sensor should show correlated detections ending in a write-storm.
steps: C2 starts first: Cobalt Strike HTTP and SMB-pipe C2 to its own team server.
Recon, credential access and lateral movement follow in order.
A large HTTPS upload to external storage follows the staging reads.
The chain ends with an SMB read/rewrite/rename storm (.play) on the file and backup servers; the ransom note is written to the shares, but the cryptography is not visible.
scenarios.notes: Shares one chain builder with the other actor scenarios; they differ in C2 style, file extension and note text. Multi-tactic; filed under its end state.

scenarios.title: Handala / Void Manticore (network-observable subset: theft + share wiper)
scenarios.expected_observation: Recon, lateral movement, a large theft and Telegram bot C2, then an SMB share wiper that overwrites files in place without renaming: a sensor should show correlated detections ending in mass overwrite.
steps: An IP-check call and Telegram Bot API long polling provide C2.
Recon and lateral movement reach the file server.
A large HTTPS upload follows the staging reads.
A share wiper overwrites files in place with random data and leaves a defacement note, with no rename; phishing delivery and local wiping are endpoint-only and absent.

scenarios.title: NeedyMantis implant (separate foothold: fixed-UA HTTPS beacon + Impacket SMB exec)
scenarios.expected_observation: A second, unrelated compromised workstation makes a fixed-user-agent HTTPS beacon and Impacket-style SMB execution against its own disjoint servers: a sensor should show a separate campaign from the other workstation scenarios.
steps: First contact carries a system-info cookie and a one-time HTTP-to-WebSocket upgrade.
Slow, jittered check-ins repeat over most of the day.
A fixed, old-looking user agent is used throughout.
Impacket-style ADMIN$ execution reaches its own server targets; the C2 host is Cloudflare-fronted so the edge address is what is on the wire.
scenarios.notes: Helper bodies (needymantis_beacon) read only by name and comments.

scenarios.title: Fast-flux / DGA C2 (algorithmic NXDOMAIN bursts, rotating A records)
scenarios.expected_observation: Bursts of NXDOMAIN lookups for algorithmic names, then a stable C2 name answered with a rotating set of addresses and a short HTTPS check-in: a sensor should flag DGA-like lookups and fast-flux answers.
steps: Several lookups of algorithmic names return NXDOMAIN.
The one stable C2 name then resolves to a different subset of a node pool each time, with a short TTL.
A short HTTPS check-in goes to the first node returned.
The pattern repeats every few minutes over the working day; the check-in body is encrypted.

scenarios.title: Infostealer exfiltration (Lumma-class credential upload to a panel)
scenarios.expected_observation: A commodity infostealer uploads a credential archive to a panel and sends a few small follow-up heartbeats: a sensor should flag one large outbound upload to a first-seen external host from a workstation.
steps: Shortly after infection the workstation resolves the panel name.
One full archive upload goes out over HTTPS.
A couple of short heartbeats follow over the next hour.
Which credentials were in the archive is not visible.
scenarios.notes: Could equally be Exfiltration (the traffic is an upload). Filed under Credential access because the payload is stolen credentials.

scenarios.title: Exposed-RDP brute force (internet → jump host, failures then a success)
scenarios.expected_observation: Many failed RDP attempts from an internet source against the exposed jump host, then one full session: a sensor should flag brute-force then success on an externally reachable RDP service.
steps: An internet address opens many short RDP connections to the jump host.
Most end in resets, one every few seconds.
The attempts cycle through a small account list.
One attempt succeeds and runs a full RDP session; passwords are not visible.

scenarios.title: Salt Typhoon network-device espionage (SNMP walks of switches/APs/sensor)
scenarios.expected_observation: A workstation walks switches, controller, sensor and other infrastructure over SNMP, slowly and repeatedly: a sensor should flag a user host doing SNMP against network infrastructure.
steps: The workstation picks one infrastructure device.
It walks that device with SNMP.
Every few minutes it picks another from a small set.
The sweep runs all window long; device configuration read is not visible beyond the SNMP traffic.

scenarios.title: Web shell on an internal server (POSTs to an odd URI, decrypted commands)
scenarios.expected_observation: An internal workstation drives a web shell on an internal web server: POSTs to an odd URI with commands in the request and output in the response, in clusters: a sensor should flag unusual POST traffic to one URI.
steps: The operator opens HTTPS to the internal web server.
A POST to an odd URI carries a command.
The response carries the command output.
Commands come in clusters of two to five with long gaps; the traffic is decryptable with the exported keys.
scenarios.notes: Category is a judgement; a web shell is also persistence or initial access in common taxonomies. Here the operator is already inside, so it is filed as a command channel.

scenarios.title: Volt Typhoon living-off-the-land (valid-account admin protocols, no malware)
scenarios.expected_observation: Valid-account use of LDAP, SMB and RDP from one workstation to a few servers at a low rate: a sensor should flag baseline deviation, not malware.
steps: The workstation makes one quiet admin touch every twenty to forty minutes.
Most touches are LDAP or SMB; one in five is RDP.
Targets are the domain controller, file server, SQL server and jump host.
There is no malware and no C2; the detection is that a workstation uses these protocols at all.

scenarios.title: Coercion → NTLM relay → AD CS → DA (ESC8)
scenarios.expected_observation: A workstation coerces a machine account over MS-EFSR, relays NTLM to the certificate authority, obtains a certificate and requests a TGT: a sensor should flag the coercion, the relay and the certificate-based logon.
steps: The relay host coerces a machine account with an MS-EFSR call over SMB.
The machine's NTLM authentication is relayed to the CA web enrollment endpoint.
A certificate is issued for the relayed identity.
A PKINIT TGT request uses that certificate. The chain repeats a few times.

scenarios.title: Edge-device exploitation → inward pivot (compromised VPN/firewall)
scenarios.expected_observation: An inbound exploit burst against the firewall, then the firewall's inside interface originates admin SMB inward and a beachhead workstation beacons out: a sensor should flag an edge device acting as a client.
steps: Three exploit requests hit the firewall from an internet address.
The firewall's inside interface then uses admin shares on servers with a harvested account.
Those pivots repeat every ten to twenty minutes.
A beachhead workstation beacons out on a fast-flux style channel; the exploit payload itself is not visible.

scenarios.title: Campaign built from threat indicators
scenarios.expected_observation: An ATT&CK-mapped campaign compiled from threat indicators or a campaign file: what a sensor sees depends on the campaign.
steps: Indicators or a campaign file are compiled into stages.
Stages are placed from the campaign's own start time.
Each action is real protocol traffic from the action catalogue.
With no campaign supplied the scenario is inert.
scenarios.notes: recipe_driven: not shown in the grid. Not one of the five named families; family is CAMPAIGN in the registry.

scenarios.title: Custom scenario rebuilt from an imported pcap recipe
scenarios.expected_observation: The flows of an imported pcap recipe are recreated in the simulated environment: what a sensor sees depends entirely on the recipe.
steps: A recipe JSON produced by the pcap importer is read.
Its hosts are mapped into the simulated environment (corp domain, users, PKI).
Each flow is rebuilt; protocols the engine cannot build are skipped and reported.
With no recipe the scenario is inert.
scenarios.notes: recipe_driven: not a default scenario, built once per imported recipe. Protocols, hosts and zones are deliberately unspecified; the lists here are placeholders.

scenarios.title: Firewall content update (Palo Alto): WHEN it ran, IF it completed, and the remote-access outage it caused
scenarios.expected_observation: A firewall bundle is pulled early and pushed later; the commit reloads the dataplane and drops the remote-access workforce for about a minute: a sensor should show the update and the VPN outage with reconnect storm.
steps: The jump host downloads the bundle before the working day.
An admin pushes it later.
The roughly 90-second commit drops every VPN tunnel; dead-peer detection gets no answer.
Tunnels rebuild within seconds of return and traffic resumes in a reconnect storm.
scenarios.notes: Category stretch: an outage event rather than slowness. Read the builder body but not the download and push helpers.

scenarios.title: Post-quantum readiness: which hosts can use PQC key exchange, which do, and which cannot
scenarios.expected_observation: TLS 1.3 handshakes across PQC-capable, PQC-using and not-capable hosts: a sensor should report post-quantum key-exchange readiness by host.
steps: Capable clients offer a hybrid group first.
PQC-ready servers select it, so sessions are using PQC.
Legacy servers choose a classical group, so capable clients are not using it.
Not-capable clients never offer one; no fault, a readiness view.
scenarios.notes: Not a fault at all; the taxonomy has no readiness bucket. Capacity is a placeholder; Weak TLS under the crypto family is the closer conceptual home.

scenarios.title: SQL Server service failure (degrade/outage/recover)
scenarios.expected_observation: The SQL Server service degrades, then fails outright, then recovers while the host stays up: a sensor should show rising database errors and drops, with ping and RDP still working.
steps: Pooled web-to-database connections get slow.
Some users see errors as the backend degrades.
The service goes down; logins and queries fail while ICMP and RDP keep working.
The admin restarts the service and traffic recovers.
scenarios.notes: Only the first 20 lines of the 90-line builder were read; the steps follow its docstring phases. Window times are absolute in the code but are not shown here.

scenarios.title: DNS degradation on EXL-DC1 (timeouts, SERVFAIL, failover)
scenarios.expected_observation: Workstation lookups to the primary domain controller time out or return SERVFAIL, with retries and failover to the secondary: a sensor should show slow and failed DNS from one resolver.
steps: Healthy lookups before the fault.
Lookups to the primary slow down or time out.
Some return SERVFAIL; clients retry and fail over to the secondary.
Recovery follows the severity envelope; there is no cause on the wire.
scenarios.notes: Faults share a sev() envelope: healthy lead-in, ramp to a plateau, then recovery.

scenarios.title: SMB file-server slowdown (zero-window, high service time)
scenarios.expected_observation: File-server reads get slow with zero-window stalls and high service time: a sensor should show high SMB response time and receiver-window stalls toward one file server.
steps: Fast reads flank the fault.
Reads against the file server slow down.
Zero-window stalls appear at peak.
Service time recovers at the end; the server-side cause is not visible.
scenarios.notes: Faults share a sev() envelope: healthy lead-in, ramp to a plateau, then recovery.

scenarios.title: WAN congestion (high RTT, retransmissions on egress)
scenarios.expected_observation: Egress HTTPS shows elevated round-trip time and retransmissions: a sensor should show WAN-side latency and retransmits to internet destinations.
steps: Fast egress before the fault.
Round-trip time rises.
Segments are retransmitted as loss increases.
Egress recovers at the end.
scenarios.notes: Faults share a sev() envelope: healthy lead-in, ramp to a plateau, then recovery. Could also be Capacity; filed with loss because retransmission is the visible symptom.

scenarios.title: Authentication latency (slow Kerberos on EXL-DC1)
scenarios.expected_observation: Kerberos logons slow down because the KDC answers late: a sensor should show high Kerberos response time to the domain controller.
steps: Fast logons before the fault.
AS-REQ to AS-REP time rises.
Service ticket requests slow as well.
Logons recover afterwards.
scenarios.notes: Faults share a sev() envelope: healthy lead-in, ramp to a plateau, then recovery. Category is a stretch: this is core-service latency, not DNS or DHCP. Taxonomy has no better home.

scenarios.title: Web-server degradation (EXL-WEB2 cascade from slow SQL1)
scenarios.expected_observation: Web-server page time tracks slow SQL queries, with some 503 responses: a sensor should show web latency whose cause is database time.
steps: Pages load fast before the fault.
The web server's database pool slows.
Page time follows database time and some return 503.
Recovery; the database is the root cause.
scenarios.notes: Faults share a sev() envelope: healthy lead-in, ramp to a plateau, then recovery.

scenarios.title: Wireless degradation (EXL-WLC1 control-plane issue)
scenarios.expected_observation: The wireless controller stalls: APs see late or lost CAPWAP echoes, rejoin in waves, and clients drop and then burst DHCP and DNS: a sensor should show control-plane loss and rejoin storms.
steps: Echo responses arrive late or not at all.
APs that wait out retransmissions rejoin (Discovery, DTLS, Join, Configuration).
Their clients drop for about a minute and a half.
Clients renew addresses and re-resolve names in a burst; a configuration-saved syslog message precedes the fault.
scenarios.notes: Zone placement of the controller and APs not confirmed from code.

scenarios.title: Web degradation from DNS (10 hosts, slow/failed resolution)
scenarios.expected_observation: Ten named workstations see slow page loads because DNS resolution slows or fails: a sensor should show DNS failures correlated with web stalls for those hosts.
steps: Each of the ten hosts loads pages fine before the fault.
DNS answers slow or fail.
Page loads stall behind resolution.
Recovery follows the envelope.
scenarios.notes: Faults share a sev() envelope: healthy lead-in, ramp to a plateau, then recovery.

scenarios.title: VoIP call-quality degradation (RTP jitter, loss, reorder)
scenarios.expected_observation: Calls between handsets show RTP jitter, loss and reordering: a sensor should show degraded call quality scores.
steps: A clean call before the fault.
SIP sets up calls between handset pairs.
RTP shows jitter, loss and reordering.
RTCP reports poor quality; recovery follows.
scenarios.notes: Faults share a sev() envelope: healthy lead-in, ramp to a plateau, then recovery.

scenarios.title: TCP retransmission / packet-loss storm on a segment
scenarios.expected_observation: Retransmits, duplicate ACKs and fast retransmits on the path to the file server after a workstation SSHes into a switch: a sensor should flag both the loss and the odd SSH source.
steps: A workstation SSHes into the switch, an unusual source for admin.
Downloads from the file server run clean before the fault.
Duplicate ACKs and retransmits climb on the path.
Loss recovers at the end; the cause is stated in code as a duplex mismatch, which is not visible.
scenarios.notes: Faults share a sev() envelope: healthy lead-in, ramp to a plateau, then recovery. Auto-selects ndr-salt-typhoon (SCENARIO_DEPENDENCIES). Downloads are SMB, not HTTP.

scenarios.title: NTP time-sync failure (EXL-NTP1 unreachable)
scenarios.expected_observation: Clients poll the time server and get no answer; clocks drift and Kerberos starts failing with clock-skew errors: a sensor should show unanswered NTP and then Kerberos errors.
steps: Healthy NTP syncs before the fault.
The server stops answering the scenario's polls.
About a third of user machines drift by seconds per minute.
Once a clock is more than five minutes off, its Kerberos requests fail with skew errors.
scenarios.notes: Faults share a sev() envelope: healthy lead-in, ramp to a plateau, then recovery. Category stretch: time sync is not DNS or DHCP.

scenarios.title: HTTP 5xx error-rate surge (LOB API on EXL-WEB2)
scenarios.expected_observation: The line-of-business API returns 500, 502 and 503 at volume while service time stays low: a sensor should show a status-code mix spike.
steps: Normal responses before the fault.
5xx responses start to appear.
At peak the status mix is dominated by 500, 502 and 503.
Service time stays low throughout; recovery follows.
scenarios.notes: Faults share a sev() envelope: healthy lead-in, ramp to a plateau, then recovery.

scenarios.title: DHCP scope exhaustion (clients cannot get a lease)
scenarios.expected_observation: DHCP discovers get no offer and requests are NAKed after a workstation RDPs to the domain controller: a sensor should flag both the lease failures and the odd RDP source.
steps: A workstation RDPs into the domain controller, an admin protocol it never uses.
Lease attempts work before the fault.
DISCOVERs get no OFFER and REQUESTs are NAKed.
Recovery follows; narrowing the scope is not visible.
scenarios.notes: Faults share a sev() envelope: healthy lead-in, ramp to a plateau, then recovery. Auto-selects ndr-volt-typhoon.

scenarios.title: Database connection-pool exhaustion (EXL-SQL1 saturated, not down)
scenarios.expected_observation: A demand surge opens more database connections than the pool allows: a sensor should show a burst of new connections to the web server, queued TDS logins and resource errors.
steps: A burst of 24 to 40 workstations hit the web server at once.
The app tier opens more database connections.
Login queues, query time climbs and some requests abort with a resource error.
The database is saturated, not down.
scenarios.notes: Faults share a sev() envelope: healthy lead-in, ramp to a plateau, then recovery.

scenarios.title: RADIUS / 802.1X NAC auth-failure storm (NPS on EXL-DC1)
scenarios.expected_observation: Access-Reject surge, dropped requests with retransmits and slow Access-Accepts on 802.1X: a sensor should show RADIUS failures during onboarding.
steps: Normal EAP exchanges before the fault.
Rejects increase.
Requests drop and retransmit.
Accepts slow; recovery follows.
scenarios.notes: Faults share a sev() envelope: healthy lead-in, ramp to a plateau, then recovery. Category stretch: NAC authentication, not DNS or DHCP.

scenarios.title: NFS / NAS storage latency (EXL-BACKUP1)
scenarios.expected_observation: NFSv3 GETATTR and READ service time climbs on port 2049 after an admin SSH to the NAS: a sensor should show high NFS latency from one server.
steps: The admin SSHes from the jump host into the NAS.
A job starts, loading the storage.
NFS read and attribute calls take longer.
Reads stall at peak; recovery follows.
scenarios.notes: Faults share a sev() envelope: healthy lead-in, ramp to a plateau, then recovery.

scenarios.title: SMTP mail-flow backup / delivery latency (relay EXL-BACKUP1)
scenarios.expected_observation: SMTP reply latency climbs and 451 greylisting backs the queue up after an admin SSH reload of the relay: a sensor should show slow mail transactions and deferrals.
steps: An admin SSHes from the jump host into the relay and reloads Postfix.
SMTP reply latency rises.
A growing share of messages get 450, 451 or 421 deferrals.
Deferred messages are resent later by the same host.
scenarios.notes: Faults share a sev() envelope: healthy lead-in, ramp to a plateau, then recovery. Category stretch: queue backup is the closest fit to Capacity.

scenarios.title: MTU blackhole / PMTUD failure (bulk flows stall to EXL-WEB2)
scenarios.expected_observation: Small requests succeed but oversized DF segments are dropped and ICMP fragmentation-needed does not lower the MSS: a sensor should show stalled bulk flows and the ICMP messages.
steps: The admin SSHes into the firewall (the stated cause).
Small requests work.
Large DF segments are dropped and ICMP fragmentation-needed appears.
The sender never lowers its MSS, so bulk flows stall.
scenarios.notes: Faults share a sev() envelope: healthy lead-in, ramp to a plateau, then recovery.

scenarios.title: OT: unauthorized Modbus write / setpoint tampering (writes to a read-only PLC)
scenarios.expected_observation: A compromised engineering workstation issues Modbus write function codes to PLCs that normally only serve reads: a sensor should flag control writes from an unexpected source.
steps: The workstation connects to a PLC that normally only answers reads.
The first write to each PLC follows a read.
Most writes are FC6, with some FC16 and FC5 and an occasional exception.
Each PLC gets its own small reused register pool; the physical effect is not visible.
scenarios.notes: Requires the OT subnet to be generated (ot_only).

scenarios.title: OT: safety-system (SIS) tampering (TRITON-shape writes to a safety controller)
scenarios.expected_observation: Modbus/TCP contact with the safety system, which should essentially never be touched: a sensor should flag any conversation with the safety controller.
steps: A host opens a Modbus/TCP session to the safety controller.
It reads registers outside the normal poll map.
A conversation with this device is itself the signal.
The real TriStation shape used by TRITON is not reproduced.
scenarios.notes: Requires the OT subnet to be generated (ot_only). The docstring itself says the TRITON protocol shape is not reproduced.

scenarios.title: OT: cross-Purdue zone violation (IT host talks straight to a Level-1 PLC)
scenarios.expected_observation: An IT host speaks Modbus directly to a Level-1 PLC, bypassing the jump host: a sensor should flag a cross-zone flow that is not from the permitted initiator.
steps: A compromised IT host connects straight to a field PLC.
Each session is one request and one response.
It reads a register range the baseline pollers never touch.
The permitted initiator (the jump host) is not involved.
scenarios.notes: Requires the OT subnet to be generated (ot_only). zone_path lists the IT side as user; the docstring says Level 4, exact subnet not read.

scenarios.title: OT: device enumeration (Modbus unit sweep, BACnet reads, DNP3 probes)
scenarios.expected_observation: The jump host sweeps the OT assets over Modbus, BACnet and DNP3: a sensor should flag device enumeration across industrial protocols.
steps: A Modbus unit and function-code sweep of the PLCs.
A BACnet Who-Is discovery sweep of the field devices.
DNP3 link-status checks reach the RTUs.
DNP3 reads follow; device identity is learned only from the replies.
scenarios.notes: Requires the OT subnet to be generated (ot_only).

scenarios.title: OT: rogue / previously-unseen device on the OT segment
scenarios.expected_observation: A new MAC and IP appears on the OT VLAN and polls a PLC as a Modbus master: a sensor should flag a previously unseen asset on a static segment.
steps: The device announces itself with an ARP probe and a gratuitous ARP.
It opens Modbus sessions to a PLC.
It sticks to a small recurring set of targets.
It was never in the baseline asset set.
scenarios.notes: Requires the OT subnet to be generated (ot_only). Category is a stretch: no taxonomy entry fits a rogue device cleanly.

scenarios.title: OT/IoT: IP camera outbound beacon (Mirai-shape egress)
scenarios.expected_observation: An IP camera that should only talk to its recorder beacons to an internet cloud: a sensor should flag egress from a camera.
steps: The camera resolves a cloud name.
It makes a fixed small check-in to one path.
A device user agent and the camera's own embedded TLS fingerprint are used.
A short JSON reply comes back; this is the IoT-botnet shape.
scenarios.notes: Requires the OT subnet to be generated (ot_only).

scenarios.title: OT: PLC unresponsive to supervisory polls (Modbus exceptions, then timeouts)
scenarios.expected_observation: A PLC stops answering SCADA polls: slave-busy exceptions first, then no reply and retransmits: a sensor should show loss of view for one controller.
steps: One long Modbus connection polls every one to two seconds.
The PLC returns slave-busy exceptions.
Replies stop and TCP retransmits follow.
After repeated timeouts the connection is closed and reopened.
scenarios.notes: Requires the OT subnet to be generated (ot_only). Category stretch; not part of the default 58.

scenarios.title: php2shell PHP core RCE (CVE-2026-109618 / -109619): internet → internal PHP server
scenarios.expected_observation: Internet recon and exploit attempts against an internal PHP server (worker-crash resets, memory leaks), then a 200, an outbound callback and web-shell commands: a sensor should flag the exploitation pattern and the server calling out.
steps: A short burst of PHP fingerprinting GETs.
Interleaved out-of-memory and session-upload-progress POSTs, mostly ending in worker-crash resets, with memory-disclosure responses.
A breakthrough request returns 200 and the server calls out.
Hands-on web-shell commands follow in clusters; the CVE labels are generator-owned models, not a real exploit shape.
scenarios.notes: The CVE identifiers are fictional in the capture; do not present them as real advisories.

scenarios.title: OT: sanctioned operator setpoint writes + logons (BENIGN baseline for the control-writes table)
scenarios.expected_observation: Sanctioned operator setpoint writes, a few benign OT logons and one after-hours item, all benign: a sensor's control-writes and logon tables should show a normal baseline so the attack scenarios stand out.
steps: One dedicated HMI writes setpoints to a PLC over a small reused register range.
A couple of benign OT NTLM logons run to a file server.
Failed Kerberos pre-authentications appear at shift change (mistyped password).
One after-hours item is included; nothing in it is an attack.
scenarios.notes: Requires the OT subnet to be generated (ot_only). This is a BENIGN baseline add-on, not a security scenario. The fixed taxonomy has no honest category for it; Impact is a placeholder that the engine owner should replace (suggest a dedicated 'Baseline' bucket or exclude it from the security rail). Behaviour read from the docstring only.

scenarios.title: OT: newly-seen pair (unknown engineering laptop appears in Zone 2 and polls+writes a PLC)
scenarios.expected_observation: An unknown engineering laptop appears in the supervisory zone, reads a PLC it has never touched, then writes a register: a sensor should flag a new client-to-PLC pair and the read-to-write escalation.
steps: The laptop appears and announces itself by ARP and name-service chatter.
It reads a PLC it has never talked to.
Reads continue low and slow while it learns the register map.
It finally writes a register.
scenarios.notes: Requires the OT subnet to be generated (ot_only).

scenarios.title: OT: egress from a field device (Zone-1 RTU resolves + beacons to the internet, rogue firmware)
scenarios.expected_observation: A field RTU resolves a first-seen internet domain and makes low-and-slow cleartext HTTP requests out: a sensor should flag egress from a control-zone device.
steps: The field device resolves a first-seen domain.
It makes cleartext HTTP requests to an internet address.
The rate is low and slow.
A control-zone asset has no reason to do either.
scenarios.notes: Requires the OT subnet to be generated (ot_only).

scenarios.title: OT: short-burst protocol sweep (Level-3 host sweeps Level-1 with sub-second connections)
scenarios.expected_observation: A Level-3 host sweeps Level-1 assets with sub-second connections: a sensor should show connection fan-out and churn rather than sustained polling.
steps: The host cycles Modbus unit IDs across every PLC.
Each probe is its own short-lived connection.
Each PLC answers only for its own unit ID; other IDs draw exceptions.
DNP3 probes then run across the RTUs.
scenarios.notes: Requires the OT subnet to be generated (ot_only).

scenarios.title: Diurnal shape: nightly backup window (bulk SMB from servers to the backup server)
scenarios.expected_observation: Several Windows servers push bulk SMB backups to the backup server in a late-evening window: a sensor should show an expected nightly byte spike in a by-hour view.
steps: Servers begin pushing late in the day.
Bulk SMB flows run to the backup server.
The by-hour byte view shows a spike.
It ends before the night; this is an expected shape, not a fault.
scenarios.notes: Opt-in diurnal shape; not a fault.

scenarios.title: Weak TLS (TLS 1.0 / RC4) on an internal service
scenarios.expected_observation: Windows clients negotiate TLS 1.0 with an RC4 cipher to a legacy internal web server: a sensor should flag deprecated protocol versions and weak ciphers.
steps: A Windows client resolves the legacy name.
It sends a legacy ClientHello.
The server picks TLS 1.0 with RC4.
Sessions repeat across the day; macOS clients are excluded because they cannot offer RC4.

scenarios.title: Expired / self-signed certificates on an internal service
scenarios.expected_observation: An internal portal and console present expired or self-signed certificates, and some first attempts abort at the warning: a sensor should flag certificate validity problems.
steps: The client connects to the portal or console.
The server sends an expired or self-signed certificate.
Some first attempts close right after the Certificate, before key exchange.
The user clicks through a few seconds later and the retry completes.

scenarios.title: Plaintext credentials (HTTP Basic, FTP, LDAP simple bind)
scenarios.expected_observation: Credentials cross the network in the clear over HTTP Basic, FTP and LDAP simple bind: a sensor should flag cleartext authentication.
steps: A client picks one of three cleartext services.
It sends HTTP Basic, a USER and PASS pair or an LDAP simple bind.
The server accepts.
Credentials are readable on the wire.
scenarios.notes: Category stretch: there is no TLS at all, which is the weakest transport.

scenarios.title: Anonymous FTP on a smart board (internal and inbound from the internet)
scenarios.expected_observation: A smart board runs an unmanaged FTP server that accepts anonymous login from inside and from the internet: a sensor should flag an unexpected FTP service and anonymous sessions.
steps: Nine internal sessions log in as anonymous with a mail-style password.
They list and fetch or store files.
Six inbound internet sessions probe with LIST and at most one small RETR.
Everything is in clear text; the firewall pinhole is inferred from the inbound sessions.
scenarios.notes: Category stretch: not a certificate problem. The fixed taxonomy has no cleartext-service bucket; flag for the owner.

scenarios.title: NetScaler Compromise (webshell → beacon → DTLS → replay → exfil → LDAP SPN scan → SMB → reverse SSH)
scenarios.expected_observation: A gateway webshell, outbound beacon, DTLS burst, session replay, config exfil, LDAP SPN scan, SMB failures and reverse SSH: the scenario is designed so that one detection (the LDAP SPN scan) fires.
steps: Webshell and C2 beacon from the gateway appear over a benign portal day.
DTLS probe and burst, then first-seen C2 DNS (NXDOMAIN) and a replayed portal session cookie.
A cleartext config upload and an LDAP enumeration plus SPN scan from the gateway's own address.
SMB session-setup failures and an SSH test then reverse SSH close the chain; TLS payloads need the exported keys.
scenarios.notes: Phase list read from build(); fingerprint fidelity limits are stated in the note.

scenarios.title: NetScaler CVE-2026-88771 (exploit → webshell → C2 beacon → LDAP SPN scan → SMB → TDS/MSSQL pivot)
scenarios.expected_observation: An unauthenticated RCE drops a webshell on the gateway, which beacons on 8443, exfils its config and pivots with a cleartext LDAP SPN scan, SMB failures and a TDS login to SQL1: a sensor should show an edge device originating admin protocols inward.
steps: Exploit then webshell write on the gateway.
The gateway beacons on 8443 with first-seen C2 DNS and exfils the stolen config.
A cleartext LDAP SPN scan hits the domain controller.
SMB session-setup failures and a TDS/MSSQL login enumerate the database; xp_cmdshell is blocked.
scenarios.notes: Steps follow the registry note and function names; the exploit shape is a model, not a real exploit (code comment).

scenarios.title: BeyondTrust CVE-2026-102764 (origin-spoofed file ops → webshell → C2 → inward RDP/SMB/LDAP pivot)
scenarios.expected_observation: An origin-spoofed request reads a secret and writes a webshell on the published appliance, which beacons, exfils its session store and then reaches inward with LDAP, SMB, RDP and SSH: a sensor should show a DMZ device acting as a client.
steps: Origin-spoofed file read and write on the appliance.
A webshell beacons on 8443 with first-seen C2 DNS.
The session store is exfiltrated.
The appliance then originates LDAP SPN scan, SMB failures, RDP to the jump host and SSH to a server.
scenarios.notes: Steps follow the registry note and function names.

scenarios.title: Metabase CVE-2026-72898 (unauth /reset_password SQLi → admin takeover → bulk TDS exfil from SQL1)
scenarios.expected_observation: An unauthenticated SQLi takes over the BI host as admin, which then pulls stored database credentials and runs bulk TDS queries against SQL1, exporting to the attacker: a sensor should flag anomalous bulk TDS from the BI server.
steps: A SQLi POST to the password-reset path takes over the admin account.
The admin API reads the connected database's stored credentials.
The BI host opens a pool to SQL1 and runs bulk queries.
The results are exported to the attacker.
scenarios.notes: Steps follow the registry note and function names.

scenarios.title: SharePoint ToolShell CVE-2026-58644 (ToolPane RCE → spinstall0 webshell + MachineKey theft → DB/DC pivot)
scenarios.expected_observation: A ToolPane POST drops a webshell, the machine key is stolen for forged ViewState commands, the host beacons and exfils, then pivots to the content DB, directory and DC: a sensor should show web-tier to database and directory pivots.
steps: ToolPane exploit with the tell-tale referer drops a webshell.
The farm machine key is stolen and used for forged ViewState commands.
The host beacons on 8443 and exfils keys and documents.
It pulls the content database over TDS, runs an LDAP SPN scan and SMB to the DC.
scenarios.notes: Steps follow the registry note and function names.

scenarios.title: PAN-OS GlobalProtect CVE-2026-0257 (forged auth-override cookie → unauthorized VPN → RDP/SMB/LDAP lateral)
scenarios.expected_observation: A forged auth-override cookie stands up an unauthorised VPN session; internal recon, LDAP SPN scan, SMB probes and RDP to the jump host then originate from the assigned VPN address: a sensor should show lateral movement from a VPN pool address.
steps: A forged auth-override cookie on the portal bypasses authentication.
The gateway assigns an internal VPN address.
Recon and an LDAP SPN scan originate from that address.
SMB probes of the DC and file server, then RDP to the jump host (the ransomware precursor).
scenarios.notes: Steps follow the registry note and function names.

scenarios.title: VMware vCenter CVE-2026-59310 (syslog traversal → cron RCE → reverse SSH → ESXi ransomware push)
scenarios.expected_observation: A syslog traversal writes a cron file on the vCenter, which dials reverse SSH out, beacons, exfils the VM inventory and then drives every ESXi host on 443 and 902 to deploy ransomware: a sensor should show reverse SSH and management-plane fan-out.
steps: A traversal request writes a cron file on the appliance.
The appliance dials reverse SSH and beacons on 8443 with first-seen C2 DNS.
The VM inventory is exfiltrated.
vCenter pushes the payload to each ESXi host over 443 and 902; no visible encryption stage beyond the push (code comment).
scenarios.notes: Steps follow the registry note and function names.

scenarios.title: WordPress upgrade-window race (CVE-2026-119977): staged setup-config.php -> rogue MySQL takeover
scenarios.expected_observation: Hours of mostly-404 polling for a staged installer, an admin-triggered core update, a short window where the same GET returns 200, then an exploit POST that points the site at an attacker MySQL server: a sensor should show web-server-originated MySQL to an external host.
steps: Background scanners poll the staged setup path and get 404.
An admin triggers a core update and the package downloads.
For a few seconds the same polling GET returns 200 and one scanner posts the setup step with attacker DB settings.
The web server now keeps talking to the attacker MySQL; benign look-alikes are included.
scenarios.notes: Steps follow the registry note; the module's own comments state that several failure variants are kept unused.

scenarios.title: Linux IPv4 TCP use-after-free race (CVE-2026-98432): IP-options SYN retry spray -> MPTCP listener leak and callback
scenarios.expected_observation: Two internet sources spray SYNs with IPv4 options at two Linux hosts; one never completes, the other loses a race, takes a payload and calls back: a sensor should show option-bearing SYN retransmits and a high-port callback.
steps: Option-bearing SYNs are retransmitted with the same port and sequence number for about fifty minutes.
The plain listener never completes a handshake and the attacker sends RSTs.
The MPTCP host loses one race: the SYN-ACK carries extra option bytes and one small payload is sent.
The host calls back to the attacker on a high port; the code marks the extra bytes and the callback as assumed, not documented.
scenarios.notes: Retransmit gap, rate and leak are modelling choices per the registry note.

scenarios.title: ARMORY CASTLE vCenter chain (CVE-2026-123890): edge-appliance exploit -> internal pivot -> vmdir bypass -> SSO admin -> secrets theft
scenarios.expected_observation: An edge appliance is exploited, an internal appliance then drives LDAP writes against the vCenter directory and logs in with the new account: a sensor should show an accepted empty-password LDAP bind, directory writes from a non-admin host, and large uploads to the same external sink.
steps: The edge appliance is exploited (file read/write, webshell) and beacons out.
The edge appliance SSHes to an internal Linux appliance, which beacons on its own.
The appliance binds to the vCenter directory with an empty password (accepted), adds an SSO user into Administrators and searches tenant credentials, then logs in with the new account.
Secrets leave over HTTP, then in bulk.
scenarios.notes: Steps follow the registry note and the pack's builder functions.

scenarios.title: Outlook NTLM hash leak (CVE-2026-124194): crafted message -> outbound SMB/WebDAV NTLM to an external host -> portal spray
scenarios.expected_observation: Workstations send NTLM authentication to an external address over SMB and HTTP, and the same account then appears at the mail portal from the internet: a sensor should flag outbound NTLM to an external host and the later spray.
steps: Workstations resolve a never-seen external name.
Each opens outbound SMB 445 and completes an NTLM exchange that the server refuses.
The WebDAV fallback repeats the NTLM exchange over HTTP on port 80.
The harvested account is sprayed and then used at the mail portal.
scenarios.notes: Steps follow the registry note and the pack's builder functions.

scenarios.title: FreeSWITCH SIP MESSAGE command injection (CVE-2026-116779): scanner sweep -> MESSAGE to the api handler -> callback -> toll fraud
scenarios.expected_observation: A call server receives SIP MESSAGE requests aimed at its api handler and then starts outbound calls and callbacks it never made before: a sensor should show the MESSAGE pattern and the toll-fraud call bursts.
steps: Scanners sweep the SIP port with OPTIONS and REGISTER.
One source sends SIP MESSAGE requests addressed to the api handler.
The call server fetches a stager over HTTP and beacons.
The call server places outbound calls to a premium-rate gateway.
scenarios.notes: Steps follow the registry note and the pack's builder functions.

scenarios.title: OPTIMJACK third-party-script skimmer: tampered experimentation-platform script -> card/cookie/wallet exfil from visitors
scenarios.expected_observation: The same script URL grows and changes while visitors start contacting new external domains with POSTs: a sensor should show first-seen servers, a size change on a stable URL and the POST bursts.
steps: Browsers load a retail site and the CDN project script.
The script URL returns a larger rebuilt body for a stretch.
Browsers contact first-seen skimmer domains with cookie beacons, card-shaped POSTs and a wallet POST.
The script returns to normal size.
scenarios.notes: Steps follow the registry note and the pack's builder functions.

scenarios.title: Puppet report-processing RCE (CVE-2026-115731): enrol + impersonate -> oversized report -> server callback, SSH, CA-key exfil
scenarios.expected_observation: A configuration server starts making outbound calls, SSH sessions and a cleartext key upload after an external agent's odd report: a sensor should show the server's new roles and the large fleet pulls.
steps: Nodes check in on port 8140 as usual.
An external agent enrols and asks for another node's catalog under that node's name.
It sends an oversized report the server takes seconds to process.
The server fetches a stager, beacons, opens SSH to nodes and sends the CA key out; nodes then pull an unusually large catalog and file.
scenarios.notes: Steps follow the registry note and the pack's builder functions.

scenarios.title: OpenSSH 'SSHole' auth bypass (CVE-2026-123158): botnet SSH wave -> bypass -> script fetch -> Stratum cryptomining
scenarios.expected_observation: A Linux host takes a wave of short SSH connections from varied clients, then starts cryptomining traffic: a sensor should show the HASSH variety, the long sessions and the Stratum login and share submissions.
steps: Five sources send short SSH connections with three different client libraries.
A few connections succeed and stay open.
The host fetches a script over HTTP.
The host resolves a pool name and speaks Stratum on port 3333.
scenarios.notes: Steps follow the registry note and the pack's builder functions.

scenarios.title: Turla Exchange-resident implant (mail-borne C2 pattern; ESET 'Cereal' toolset): task mail in -> server replies out -> bulk collected-mail archives to a first-seen MX
scenarios.expected_observation: The mail server itself sends mail to an address no user mails, right after each inbound task message, and ships large archives out: a sensor should show the new outbound destination and the cadence.
steps: An external sender mails small attachments to one service mailbox.
The Exchange server replies by outbound SMTP to a first-seen mail host.
It sends large archive attachments at a steady cadence.
Ordinary partner mail continues.
scenarios.notes: Steps follow the registry note and the pack's builder functions. ESET describes Cereal as an Exchange-resident toolset with no attacker-controlled server whose backdoor answers Exchange-looking web requests; the mail-borne tasking and outbound-SMTP replies replayed here are the older Turla Exchange-implant pattern (LightNeuron, 2019), used as the network-observable stand-in.

scenarios.title: The Gentlemen ransomware kill chain (vendor threat reports; no CISA advisory)
scenarios.expected_observation: A ransomware chain with its own team server, rclone-style exfiltration and a .gentlemen extension: a sensor should show the staged chain ending in mass SMB rewrites.
steps: Reconnaissance, credential access and lateral movement from the foothold.
Cobalt Strike HTTP and SMB-pipe beacons to a dedicated team server.
Data theft with an rclone user agent.
SMB encryption write-storm with a .gentlemen extension and ransom note.
scenarios.notes: Steps follow the registry note and the pack's builder functions.

scenarios.title: IPv6 rogue RA + DHCPv6 takeover (mitm6 style)
scenarios.expected_observation: A workstation advertises itself with Router Advertisements, answers DHCPv6 with its own address as the DNS server, serves a proxy-discovery file over IPv6 and collects NTLM authentication, then reuses that identity against a file server over IPv4: a sensor should flag the rogue router, the DHCPv6 server that is not a server, and the relayed authentication.
steps: The attacker sends Router Advertisements with the managed and other-configuration flags set and no default router, repeating them through the window.
A victim asks for DHCPv6 configuration and the attacker answers, offering its own address as the DNS server.
The victim looks up the proxy-discovery name through the attacker, fetches the file over IPv6 and answers an NTLM challenge.
The attacker uses the captured identity to open an SMB session to a file server over IPv4.
scenarios.notes: Modelled on the public description of the mitm6 technique. The relay leg is SMB with the victim's account name, not an LDAP relay; the traffic shape (rogue router, non-server DHCPv6, NTLM to a workstation) is the finding.

scenarios.title: IPv6 neighbour-discovery flood (RA flood + NS storm)
scenarios.expected_observation: A workstation sends hundreds of Router Advertisements from random source addresses, each announcing a different prefix, then solicits addresses that do not exist so the gateway retries each one: a sensor should flag the advertisement flood and the neighbour-discovery volume.
steps: The attacker resolves its gateway through ordinary neighbour discovery.
It floods the segment with Router Advertisements, each from a new random link-local source and carrying a new prefix.
After a pause it sends Neighbor Solicitations for addresses nobody holds.
For every one of them the gateway solicits the missing address three times, a second apart.
scenarios.notes: Category is a judgement: the flood is a denial of service on the segment (impact); some taxonomies call it discovery abuse.
